title: Plain food, hard ground
hookLine: Musonius taught plain food and hard work as training (Musonius Rufus, Lectures 18–19)

cards: Count the decisions food asks of you in a day. What to order. Which of the forty cereals.
Whether the coffee has the right milk. Delivery or pickup. The next small pleasure is always one tap away, and the choosing never quite stops.
In imperial Rome, a teacher looked at the rich tables of his city, dish after imported dish, feasts that ran for hours, and gave his students some unfashionable advice.

teach.b: That teacher was Musonius Rufus, whom we met four days ago arguing that women should study philosophy.
Two of his lectures are about food, and he says something that sounds too simple: self-control at the table is the beginning and the foundation of self-control everywhere else. Why food?
Because it comes around several times a day, a test you meet over and over. His advice is concrete.
Prefer food that's cheap and easy to find: fruit, vegetables, milk, cheese, honey. Eat to nourish the body, not to chase the next flavor.
He repeats an old saying often credited to Socrates: most people live to eat, but a good person eats to live. In another lecture he turns to clothing and houses.
Clothes are for protecting the body, not for showing off; a house is for shelter from heat and cold, not for being admired.
And in a lecture on training, he says a person should get used to cold and heat, thirst and hunger, a hard bed and plain meals, not as punishment, but as practice.
The Greek word is askēsis, training, the word athletes used; it's where English gets ascetic. For Musonius, plain food isn't about being miserable, or saving money, or looking virtuous. It's a gym.
Each simple meal is a small rep that makes you less easy to push around by wanting. His point: someone content with bread and cheese is harder to bribe, easier to please, and freer.

how: Some Stoic practitioners keep simple meals and occasional small hardships, like a cold shower or a plain lunch, as training in contentment rather than as punishment.

a strict diet meant to punish the body for its wants
simple meals practiced as training in self-control

the English word ascetic comes from the Greek for training

games.q: Musonius says self-control starts somewhere specific. where?
games.why: food comes two or three times a day, so the table is a training ground you visit every day.

practice: If you have water nearby, take one slow sip; if not, just swallow, and notice: nothing fancy, and yet exactly what the body wants.
Now picture a plain meal, bread, rice, an apple, whatever is simple where you live, eaten slowly with no screen and no sauce. Notice any part of you that protests: that's the muscle.

wordCard.voice: Plain food. Musonius Rufus's training: simple meals and a little hardship, practiced so wanting has less hold on you.

orig.note: Greek: training, exercise; the root of ascetic.

carryVoice: Your line: plain is training. If you have a medical diet, it comes first. Two hundred ninety-nine days now.
